In Singapore, the results came out at noon. Ada read the paper in the school hall and felt the floor tilt. She had failed maths. Not badly, but failed. Without it, the course she wanted was out of reach.

At six her mother knocked and came in without waiting. She sat on the bed and put a hand on Ada's back. "Xin's mother called. Tell me."
Ada cried for a long time. Her mother just listened. Then she said, "Tonight we eat. Tomorrow we find out about the retake. It hurts. It is not the end."

For three days I did nothing. I skipped the canteen. I watched old cartoons. I let myself feel awful, and I told my roommate that was what I was doing, so she wouldn't worry.

Then one small thing. Not "I'll win next year." Just: I'll volunteer for the library committee this term. It took one email.
That was October. By February, people knew my name. Small things, one at a time. That felt more real than any big promise I made to myself.

When it closed, I stopped seeing friends. I told people I was "taking a break." Really I was sitting at home feeling like a fraud. I'd told everyone this would work. My dad had lent me money. I kept replaying every decision.
